notes.back: Central Processing Unit — the general-purpose processor executing instructions in a computer.
An independent processing unit within a CPU that can execute its own instruction stream; modern CPUs have many cores for parallel execution.

notes.front: What is Simultaneous Multithreading (SMT), e.g. Intel Hyper-Threading?
notes.back: A technique letting one physical core run two (or more) threads concurrently by sharing execution resources, improving utilization but not doubling performance.

notes.front: What is L1, L2, L3 cache?
notes.back: Layers of fast on-chip memory, from smallest/fastest (L1, per-core) to largest/slowest (L3, often shared across cores), buffering data between core and main memory.
A multi-CPU/multi-socket memory architecture where each CPU has local memory it accesses fast, and remote memory (attached to another CPU) it accesses slower.

notes.front: Why does NUMA matter for cloud workloads?
notes.back: Pinning processes/threads to the NUMA node holding their memory avoids costly cross-node memory traffic, which matters for high-performance and virtualized workloads.

notes.front: What is an Instruction Set Architecture (ISA)?
notes.back: The interface between hardware and software defining supported instructions, registers, and addressing modes — e.g. x86-64 or ARM.

notes.front: x86-64 vs ARM in cloud infrastructure?
notes.back: x86-64 (Intel/AMD) is CISC-derived, dominant in traditional servers; ARM is RISC-based, increasingly used in cloud (AWS Graviton) for better performance-per-watt.
The maximum heat a chip is expected to dissipate under sustained workload, in watts — used to size cooling and power infrastructure.
The physical connector on a motherboard holding a CPU package; multi-socket servers connect multiple CPUs via interconnects like Intel UPI or AMD Infinity Fabric.

notes.front: What is vCPU in cloud computing?
notes.back: A virtual CPU — a share (often one hyperthread) of a physical CPU core allocated to a virtual machine or container.
The rate (in GHz) at which a CPU executes clock cycles; higher frequency generally means faster single-threaded execution, within thermal limits.
A CPU design technique overlapping the stages (fetch, decode, execute, etc.) of multiple instructions to increase throughput.
A CPU technique that guesses the outcome of conditional branches ahead of time to keep the pipeline full, rolling back on misprediction.
Graphics Processing Unit — a massively parallel processor originally for rendering graphics, now widely used for AI training/inference.

notes.front: Why are GPUs well-suited to AI workloads?
notes.back: They contain thousands of simple cores executing the same instruction across many data elements (SIMT), matching the highly parallel matrix math in neural networks.

notes.front: What is Single Instruction, Multiple Threads (SIMT)?
notes.back: NVIDIA's execution model where groups of threads (warps) execute the same instruction in lockstep across different data, underlying GPU parallelism.
NVIDIA's general-purpose parallel processing cores that perform floating-point and integer arithmetic within a GPU streaming multiprocessor.
Specialized NVIDIA GPU units that accelerate matrix multiply-accumulate operations at reduced precision (e.g. FP16, INT8, FP8), core to AI training speed.
Video Random Access Memory — dedicated high-bandwidth memory on a GPU used to store model weights, activations, and data during computation.
A stacked DRAM technology placed very close to the GPU die (via an interposer) providing very high memory bandwidth, used in datacenter GPUs (HBM2e, HBM3).

notes.front: Why does memory bandwidth matter more than capacity for many AI workloads?
notes.back: Many AI inference/training steps are memory-bound, meaning GPU compute idles waiting on data movement; higher bandwidth keeps compute units fed.
NVIDIA's high-speed direct GPU-to-GPU interconnect, offering much higher bandwidth than PCIe for multi-GPU communication.
A switch chip enabling all-to-all NVLink connectivity among many GPUs in a single server node, so every GPU can talk to every other at full NVLink bandwidth.
PCIe (Peripheral Component Interconnect Express) is a general-purpose bus connecting GPUs to the CPU/system; NVLink is a purpose-built, much faster GPU-to-GPU link.

notes.front: What is GPU sharding / model parallelism?
notes.back: Splitting a large model's parameters or layers across multiple GPUs because it doesn't fit in one GPU's memory, requiring inter-GPU communication during compute.
Training using lower-precision formats (FP16/BF16/FP8) for most operations to save memory and increase throughput, while keeping some operations in higher precision for stability.
A 16-bit floating point format with the same exponent range as FP32 but reduced mantissa precision, popular for AI training due to stability and speed.
The core processing block of an NVIDIA GPU, containing CUDA cores, Tensor Cores, registers, and shared memory, replicated many times per chip.
GPU passthrough dedicates a physical GPU directly to one VM; vGPU (virtual GPU) time-slices or partitions a physical GPU across multiple VMs.
NVIDIA H100, H200, B200 (Blackwell); AMD MI300X — used for large-scale AI training and inference in cloud datacenters.

notes.front: What is a GPU cluster / SuperPOD?
notes.back: A tightly interconnected group of GPU servers (via NVLink/NVSwitch and InfiniBand) designed to train very large models across hundreds or thousands of GPUs.
Tensor Processing Unit — Google's custom Application-Specific Integrated Circuit (ASIC) built specifically to accelerate tensor/matrix operations for machine learning.
A grid of processing elements that pass data rhythmically between neighbors, allowing matrix multiplication to be computed with high reuse and minimal memory traffic — the core of TPU design.

notes.front: TPU vs GPU: key design difference?
notes.back: TPUs are ASICs purpose-built for matrix multiplication with systolic arrays, trading flexibility for higher efficiency on ML workloads, whereas GPUs are more general-purpose parallel processors.
A large cluster of TPU chips connected via a dedicated high-speed interconnect, functioning as a single large accelerator for distributed training on Google Cloud.

notes.front: What is an Application-Specific Integrated Circuit (ASIC)?
notes.back: A chip custom-designed for one specific function (e.g. TPU for ML matrix math) rather than general-purpose computing, offering higher efficiency but no flexibility.

notes.front: What is the TPU interconnect used within a pod?
notes.back: Google's Inter-Chip Interconnect (ICI), a dedicated high-bandwidth, low-latency mesh/torus network linking TPU chips directly without going through a CPU host.

notes.front: Why might a company choose custom AI ASICs (TPU, Trainium, etc.) over GPUs?
notes.back: Custom ASICs can offer better cost/performance and power efficiency for a specific, well-understood workload at large scale, at the cost of ecosystem flexibility (e.g. CUDA support).
Amazon's custom ASICs analogous to TPUs — Trainium for training, Inferentia for inference — designed to reduce cost per workload on AWS.

Hard Disk Drive (HDD) stores data magnetically on spinning platters with a moving read/write head; Solid State Drive (SSD) stores data electrically in flash memory with no moving parts, giving far lower latency.
Non-Volatile Memory Express — a storage protocol designed for flash/SSD storage over PCIe, offering much higher throughput and lower latency than older protocols like SATA/AHCI.
SATA (Serial ATA) is an older interface originally designed for spinning disks with limited bandwidth; NVMe uses PCIe lanes directly, enabling far higher IOPS and lower latency for SSDs.
Input/Output Operations Per Second — a measure of how many read/write operations a storage device or system can handle per second.

notes.front: Block storage vs Object storage vs File storage?
notes.back: Block storage exposes raw addressable blocks (like a virtual disk, e.g. EBS); object storage stores immutable objects with metadata accessed via HTTP APIs (e.g. S3); file storage exposes a hierarchical filesystem shared over a network (e.g. NFS).

notes.front: What is Redundant Array of Independent Disks (RAID)?
notes.back: A technique combining multiple physical disks into one logical unit for redundancy and/or performance, using schemes like RAID 0 (striping), RAID 1 (mirroring), RAID 5/6 (parity).
A RAID level striping data with distributed parity across at least 3 disks, tolerating failure of one disk while balancing capacity and redundancy.
A data protection technique (used in distributed/object storage) that splits data into fragments with added parity fragments, tolerating multiple failures with less overhead than full replication.

notes.front: What is a Storage Area Network (SAN)?
notes.back: A dedicated network providing block-level storage access to servers, typically over Fibre Channel or iSCSI, decoupling storage from compute.
A storage device/service providing file-level access over a standard network (e.g. via NFS or SMB), simpler to manage than a SAN but typically lower performance.

notes.front: What is data tiering in cloud storage?
notes.back: Automatically moving data between storage classes (hot, cool, cold, archive) based on access frequency to optimize cost versus latency.
An open-source distributed storage system providing object, block, and file storage on a single cluster, commonly used to build storage backends for Kubernetes and OpenStack.

notes.front: What is a persistent volume in Kubernetes?
notes.back: An abstraction representing a piece of storage provisioned for a cluster, decoupled from any individual pod's lifecycle, backed by underlying storage like a SAN, NAS, or cloud disk.

notes.front: Why is storage often the bottleneck in AI training pipelines?
notes.back: Feeding large datasets to GPUs fast enough (data loading throughput) can lag behind GPU compute speed, requiring high-throughput parallel filesystems or local NVMe caching.
A high-throughput, low-latency networking technology (often used with RDMA) common in High-Performance Computing (HPC) and large AI training clusters for GPU-to-GPU communication across nodes.

notes.front: What is Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA)?
notes.back: A technology letting one machine read/write another machine's memory directly, bypassing the CPU and OS kernel, drastically reducing latency and CPU overhead.

notes.front: What is RDMA over Converged Ethernet (RoCE)?
notes.back: A protocol implementing RDMA over standard Ethernet networks instead of InfiniBand, letting datacenters get RDMA's low latency using Ethernet infrastructure.

notes.front: What is a spine-leaf network topology?
notes.back: A two-tier datacenter network design where every leaf (top-of-rack) switch connects to every spine switch, giving predictable, non-blocking bandwidth between any two racks.
A network design where each server rack has its own switch at the top, aggregating that rack's traffic before sending it up to the spine layer.
The worst-case bandwidth available between two halves of a network if split in two — a key metric for distributed training performance across many nodes.

notes.front: What is a Network Interface Card (NIC), and what is a SmartNIC?
notes.back: A NIC connects a server to the network; a SmartNIC offloads networking, storage, or security processing (e.g. via an onboard Data Processing Unit) from the host CPU.

notes.front: What is a Data Processing Unit (DPU)?
notes.back: A programmable processor on a SmartNIC dedicated to handling networking, storage, and security tasks, freeing the host CPU/GPU for compute (e.g. NVIDIA BlueField).

notes.front: Why do large AI training clusters need specialized networking?
notes.back: Distributed training requires frequent, large gradient/parameter synchronization across nodes (all-reduce); network latency/bandwidth can become the bottleneck limiting scaling efficiency.
A collective communication pattern where every node combines (e.g. sums) values across all nodes and receives the combined result, used to synchronize gradients in distributed training.
A standard unit of rack height equal to 1.75 inches (4.45 cm); servers and switches are measured in U (e.g. 1U, 2U, 4U) to fit standard 19-inch racks.

notes.front: What is a Power Distribution Unit (PDU)?
notes.back: A device that distributes electrical power to multiple devices within a rack, often with monitoring and remote power-cycling capability.
A datacenter efficiency metric equal to total facility power divided by IT equipment power; a PUE of 1.0 would mean zero overhead from cooling/power losses.

notes.front: Why is liquid cooling increasingly used for AI infrastructure?
notes.back: High-density GPU racks generate more heat than air cooling can efficiently remove; liquid cooling (direct-to-chip or immersion) handles higher thermal density with better energy efficiency.
A cooling method circulating coolant through cold plates mounted directly on hot components (CPU/GPU), removing heat more efficiently than air alone.
A cooling method submerging entire servers/components in a dielectric (non-conductive) fluid that absorbs heat directly, used for very high-density compute.

notes.front: What is a hot aisle / cold aisle layout?
notes.back: A datacenter design alternating rows of racks so cold air intakes face one aisle and hot exhaust faces another, improving cooling efficiency.

notes.front: What is rack density measured in?
notes.back: Kilowatts (kW) per rack — traditional racks might draw 5-10kW, while dense AI GPU racks can exceed 40-100kW, driving the shift to liquid cooling.

notes.front: What is redundancy tiering (e.g. Tier III/IV datacenter)?
notes.back: A classification (Uptime Institute) of datacenter resilience based on redundant power/cooling paths and fault tolerance, from Tier I (basic) to Tier IV (fully fault-tolerant).

notes.front: What is an Uninterruptible Power Supply (UPS)?
notes.back: A battery (or flywheel) backup system providing short-term power during outages, bridging the gap until generators start or power is restored.
Software that creates and runs virtual machines by abstracting physical hardware; Type 1 (bare-metal, e.g. KVM, ESXi) runs directly on hardware, Type 2 runs atop a host OS.
A Linux kernel module turning Linux into a Type 1 hypervisor, widely used as the virtualization backbone for OpenStack and many public clouds.

notes.front: Bare metal vs virtualized cloud instances?
notes.back: Bare metal gives a tenant an entire physical server with no hypervisor overhead (common for GPU-heavy AI workloads); virtualized instances share physical hardware via a hypervisor.
An isolated location (often a distinct datacenter or set of datacenters) within a cloud region, with independent power/cooling/networking, used to build fault-tolerant architectures.
A geographic area containing multiple availability zones, letting workloads be placed close to users while zones within it provide redundancy.

notes.front: What is overprovisioning / oversubscription in cloud infrastructure?
notes.back: Allocating more virtual resources (CPU, network bandwidth) than physically exist, betting that not all tenants use their full allocation simultaneously.

notes.front: What is a container vs a virtual machine?
notes.back: A VM virtualizes hardware and runs a full guest OS via a hypervisor; a container virtualizes at the OS level, sharing the host kernel, making it lighter-weight and faster to start.

notes.front: What is bin packing in cloud/cluster scheduling?
notes.back: The scheduling problem of placing workloads (VMs, containers, pods) onto physical hosts to maximize resource utilization while respecting constraints (CPU, memory, GPU, affinity).

notes.front: What is GPU fractionalization / Multi-Instance GPU (MIG)?
notes.back: NVIDIA's technology partitioning a single physical GPU into several fully isolated instances, each with dedicated memory and compute, for multi-tenant efficiency.

notes.front: What is a Field-Programmable Gate Array (FPGA), and how does it relate to cloud infra?
notes.back: A reconfigurable chip whose logic can be rewritten after manufacturing, used in cloud for custom acceleration (networking, video transcoding, some ML inference) where ASIC-level efficiency isn't justified.

notes.front: What is total cost of ownership (TCO) in datacenter planning?
notes.back: The full cost of infrastructure including hardware purchase, power, cooling, networking, real estate, and maintenance over its lifetime — not just sticker price of servers/GPUs.

notes.front: What is capacity planning in cloud/AI infrastructure?
notes.back: Forecasting future compute, storage, and network demand to ensure enough hardware (e.g. GPUs) is procured and racked ahead of need, given long hardware lead times.
